signal.summary: Creates a writable signal: a function returning its value, with set, update and get.
signal.description:
signal() stores value in a new Signal.State and returns a Signal: a function returning the current value. A call made while a computed signal, an effect or a template binding runs also registers the signal as one of its dependencies; anywhere else, it only returns the value.

set(value) replaces the value and update(fn) computes it from the current one. Both compare the new value with the current one through equals, Object.is by default, and do nothing when they are equal. Otherwise the dependents are told synchronously that something changed, and the effects and template bindings reading the signal run again in a microtask, once for all the writes of the same synchronous block.

The type of the value is inferred from value. Pass it as a type argument when the initial value is narrower than the values to come, as in signal<User | null>(null).

Like every function of @xaendar/core/signals, it works on the global Signal that loadSignals() installs: see Installation.

members.value: The initial value, stored as it is: it is not copied, and equals is not called on it. Later writes are compared with the current value, by reference for objects and arrays, unless equals says otherwise.
members.equals:
Decides whether a new value equals the current one. Every set and update calls it synchronously, with the current value and the new one, and with this bound to the underlying Signal.State, not to the function returned by signal(). When it returns true the write is ignored: the signal keeps the old value and notifies nobody.

The default is Object.is, which compares objects and arrays by reference, not by content. Keep it a cheap, pure comparison of its two arguments: if it throws, the write throws. See SignalEqual.
members.watched:
Called when the signal goes from no dependents to one. A dependent is an effect or a template binding reading the signal, directly or through computed signals; a computed signal reading it counts as one too, from an evaluation to the next, even when nothing watches the computed signal. With unwatched, it is the place to start and stop what feeds the signal: a timer, a subscription, an event listener.

Signals are frozen while it runs: reading or writing any of them throws, so defer that work with queueMicrotask or a timer. A dependent releases its dependencies and collects them again at each of its runs, so a signal with a single dependent sees unwatched and then watched again at each of those runs: keep the two callbacks cheap, each one undoing the other.
members.unwatched: Called when the signal loses its last dependent: the effect reading it is disposed, the template binding is removed, or the computed signal reading it is evaluated again without reading it. Undo there what watched started. Signals are frozen while it runs, as in watched.

readingAndWriting.title: Reading and writing
readingAndWriting.body: Call the signal, or its get(), to read it. set replaces the value; update computes it from the current one, read without tracking, so an effect can update a signal without depending on it.

identity.title: Values are compared by reference
identity.body: Mutating the value in place — push, splice, assigning a property — goes unnoticed: the signal still holds the same reference, so nobody is notified and the templates keep showing stale data. Setting the same reference again is ignored too. Treat the values as immutable, and write new arrays and objects.

inAComponent.title: In a component
inAComponent.body: A member initialized with signal() is recognized by the template compiler as a signal: the text interpolations and the attribute bindings reading it update when it changes. So is a signal declared at module level and imported by the template with @import. A member holding a signal returned by a function of yours needs the type Signal: see Sharing state.

computed.summary: Creates a read-only signal whose value is derived from other signals, evaluated lazily when it is read.
computed.description:
computed() wraps value in a new Signal.Computed and returns a Computed: a function returning the derived value, also available as get(). It has no set and no update: to change the value, change the signals it reads.

Nothing runs when it is created. The first read runs the function and records the signals it read as dependencies. While the computed signal is watched — read by an effect or a template binding, directly or through other computed signals — its value is cached, and evaluated again only by the first read after a dependency changed. When nothing watches it, every read evaluates it again.

A change is propagated in topological order: a computed signal is evaluated after the ones it reads, and only once, so nobody sees an old value mixed with a new one. Reading a computed signal while it is being evaluated, as two computed signals reading each other do, throws Circular dependency detected while computing a Computed signal.

members.value:
The function deriving the value. Every signal it reads is a dependency, and the dependencies are collected again at each evaluation: a signal read only in a branch that was not taken is not one. Reads wrapped in untracked are not recorded.

Inside a regular function, this is the underlying Signal.Computed; an arrow function keeps the this around it, the instance in a class. Keep the function pure: it may run at any read, or never, so writes and side effects belong in an effect.
members.equals:
Decides whether a new result equals the cached one. It is called after every evaluation except the first one and the ones following an error, with the cached value and the new one, and with this bound to the underlying Signal.Computed. When it returns true, the computed signal keeps the cached value and its dependents are not told that it changed: the computed signals, the effects and the template bindings reading only it do not run again.

The default is Object.is. A comparison by content suits a function returning a new array or object at every evaluation. If equals throws, its error becomes the result, thrown by every read.

inAClass.title: In a class
inAClass.body: In a component, store the computed signal in a field: the template compiler recognizes a member initialized with computed() as a signal, so the attribute bindings reading it are reactive. Its function reads the other members through this, so it must be an arrow function, or call a method from one.

errors.title: Errors are cached
errors.body: When the function throws, the error is stored like a value: every read throws it again. While the computed signal is watched, the function does not run again until a dependency changes, and the next evaluation that succeeds clears the error.

effect.summary: Runs a function now, and again whenever a signal it read changes: the way signals reach the outside world.
effect.description:
effect() runs fn immediately and synchronously, recording the signals it reads. When one of them changes, fn runs again in a microtask, and its dependencies are collected again. It returns a function, the disposer, that stops the effect for good: the dependencies are released and fn never runs again.

The function runs inside a Signal.Computed observed by a Watcher of Signal.subtle. The watcher is told synchronously that a dependency changed, and schedules a single run for all the changes of the same synchronous block. A signal read directly that changes and then changes back still makes fn run; a computed signal whose result did not change does not.

A standalone effect lives until its disposer is called, whatever happens to the code that created it. Components and directives have their own this.effect(fn, options?), on CustomElement and CustomDirective: it takes the same arguments, and its effect is disposed when the element leaves the page. The bindings of the templates are effects too.

members.fn:
The function to run. Every signal it reads is a dependency, and the dependencies are collected again at each run; reads wrapped in untracked are not recorded. What it returns is ignored: a cleanup function returned as in other libraries is never called.

It may write signals, but writing a signal it also reads schedules a new run every time.
members.onBeforeRun: Called before every run, the first one included. A run scheduled by a change calls it even when it ends up not calling fn, because the computed signals fn reads kept their value.
members.onAfterRun: Called after every run, the first one included, even when fn throws: before the error leaves effect() or the microtask. Like onBeforeRun, it is called also when a scheduled run does not call fn.
members.onCleanup:
Called when the disposer is called, before the dependencies are released. It does not run between one run and the next: clean up after the previous run at the beginning of fn, or in onBeforeRun.

When the first run throws, no disposer is returned, and onCleanup is never called. Calling the disposer of a standalone effect a second time calls onCleanup again, then throws Cannot unwatch a signal that is not being watched.

batching.title: One run per synchronous block
batching.body: All the writes made in the same synchronous block cause a single run, in a microtask, which sees the final values.

components.title: Effects of components and directives
components.body: In a component or a directive, create effects with this.effect(), in onInit or afterRender: they are disposed when the element leaves the page. A standalone effect() created there keeps running after the element is gone, and the next connection creates another one.

errors.title: Errors
errors.body: An error thrown by the first run is thrown by effect() itself: the effect is removed and no disposer is returned. An error thrown by a later run escapes the microtask, reaches the global error handler, and the effect keeps reacting to the next changes.

loops.title: Writing a signal it reads
loops.body: An effect writing a signal it also reads schedules a new run at every run: the microtask queue never empties and the page freezes. Derive values with computed() instead. update() reads the current value without tracking it, so it is safe for the signals the effect does not read otherwise.

untracked.summary: Runs a function without recording the signals it reads as dependencies, and returns its result.
untracked.description:
untracked(fn) calls fn synchronously, with no computation in progress, and returns what it returns. The signals read inside it do not become dependencies of the computed signal, the effect or the template binding running at that moment, which therefore does not run again when they change. Outside of them, it just calls fn.

Only the reads made inside fn are untracked: the same signal read elsewhere in the same computation is still a dependency. Writes are not affected. If fn throws, the error is thrown again, and the tracking resumes as before.

It is the same function as untrack of Signal.subtle.

members.fn: The function to call. Whatever it returns is returned by untracked. Only the reads it makes synchronously are untracked: in an async function, the ones before the first await. The reads after an await happen when the computation is over, and are never tracked.

currentValue.title: Reading the current value
currentValue.body: Use it when an effect or a computed signal needs the current value of a signal, but must not run again when that signal changes.

callingCode.title: Calling code that reads signals
callingCode.body: A method called by an effect may read signals of its own, which would become dependencies of the effect. Wrapping the call leaves them out, so that only the reads written in the effect decide when it runs.

update.title: update() is already untracked
update.body: update of a Signal reads the current value with untracked: an effect can append to a signal with it without depending on that signal.

polyfill.title: Read when the module is evaluated
polyfill.body: untracked is taken from the global Signal.subtle as soon as @xaendar/core/signals is evaluated: importing the module before loadSignals() has run fails at once. Call it first, then load the rest of the application with await import(), as Installation shows.

Signal.summary: The type of the writable signals created by signal(): a function returning the value, with get, set and update.
Signal.description:
A Signal<Value> is what signal() returns. Calling it, as in count(), returns the current value and, inside a computed signal, an effect or a template binding, registers the signal as a dependency. Its methods read and change the value.

At run time it is a function carrying get, set and update, which work on an internal Signal.State. They are bound to it, so they also work when passed around on their own, as in promise.then(count.set). The function itself is not an instance of Signal.State.

Use the type to annotate a member holding a signal created somewhere else: the template compiler recognizes the members typed with the types of @xaendar/core/signals, and makes the attribute bindings reading them reactive.

members.get: Returns the current value, like calling the signal, and registers the signal as a dependency of the computed signal, the effect or the template binding running. It throws while signals are frozen, inside the watched and unwatched callbacks.
members.set: Replaces the value, unless equals, Object.is by default, finds it equal to the current one: then the call does nothing. Otherwise the dependents are notified synchronously, and the effects and template bindings reading the signal run again in a microtask. It throws while signals are frozen, and when equals throws.
members.update: Calls updater with the current value and sets what it returns, with the rules of set. The current value is read with untracked: calling update in an effect does not make the effect depend on the signal. Return a new array or object instead of changing the current one: the same reference is equal to itself, and the write would be ignored.

annotating.title: Annotating members
annotating.body: A member initialized by a function of yours returning a signal is not recognized by the template compiler: text interpolations read it, but attribute bindings are evaluated once. Annotate it with Signal imported from @xaendar/core/signals; a type alias of your own, even of the same type, is not recognized.

Computed.summary: The type of the read-only signals created by computed(): a function returning the derived value, with get.
Computed.description:
A Computed<Value> is what computed() returns. Calling it, as in total(), returns the derived value, evaluating it when needed, and registers it as a dependency of the computed signal, the effect or the template binding running. It has no set and no update.

At run time it is a function carrying get, bound to an internal Signal.Computed; the function itself is not an instance of Signal.Computed.

Use the type to annotate members and exports holding a computed signal created somewhere else: as with Signal, the template compiler then recognizes the member, and the attribute bindings reading it are reactive.

members.get: Returns the value, like calling the computed signal. It evaluates the function first when the cached value is stale, or always when nothing watches the computed signal, and throws the error of the last evaluation, if it threw one. It also throws on a circular dependency, and while signals are frozen.

readOnlyViews.title: Read-only views of a store
readOnlyViews.body: A module can keep its writable signals private, and export computed signals reading them together with the functions changing them: the other modules can read the state, not write it.

InputSignal.summary: The type of the inputs declared with @Property: a signal the parent writes through its template, and the component can only read.
InputSignal.description:
The @Property decorator, and @Property.required, go on an accessor of a component or a directive typed InputSignal<ActualValue>, and replace it with an input signal. The input holds its default value until a template binds it, then every value bound, converted by transform and compared with equals (see InputSignalOptions). When a conditional binding stops holding, it goes back to the default value.

Calling it, as in this.label(), or its get(), returns the value and tracks it like any signal: the templates, computed signals and effects reading it update when the parent binds a new value. It has no public set: only the bindings of the templates using the component write it.

The type matters at build time too: the templates binding the input are type-checked against ActualValue, and the annotation, imported from @xaendar/core/signals, tells the template compiler that the accessor is a signal.

members.get: Returns the current value, like calling the input, and registers it as a dependency of the computed signal, the effect or the template binding running.

declaring.title: Declaring inputs
declaring.body: The first argument of @Property is the default value, the second one its options: alias, the name used by the templates, and the options of the input. @Property.required() declares an input without default, that every template using the component must bind.

narrowerTypes.title: Types narrower than the default
narrowerTypes.body: TypeScript infers the type of the decorator from the default value, so a default such as 'ts', [] or null does not match a narrower type of the accessor. Pass the type of the signal to the decorator too, instead of widening the accessor and casting what you read.

readOnly.title: Read-only inside the component
readOnly.body: Writing an input from inside the component does not compile, and forced with a cast it throws. For a value the component changes too, copy the input into a local signal with an effect, and write the local one.

QuerySignal.summary: The type of the queries declared with @Query and its variants: a read-only signal holding the elements found, kept up to date by the framework.
QuerySignal.description:
The @Query decorators go on an accessor of a component typed QuerySignal<Value>, and replace it with a query signal. Value is the element found or null for @Query and @Query.content, the element for their required variants, and an array of elements for their all variants; the type of the elements is described by QueryElement.

It holds null, or an empty array, until the component is connected for the first time. At every connection the query is run right after the render, before afterRender; then a MutationObserver runs it again each time elements are added to or removed from the template or, for content queries, the projected content, and also when a slot attribute or the slots change. Other attribute changes, such as a class, are not observed. When the component leaves the page the observation stops, and the signal keeps its last result. The all variants notify only when the list of elements changes.

Calling it, or its get(), returns the result and tracks it like any signal. It has no set.

members.get: Returns the current result, like calling the query, and registers it as a dependency of the computed signal, the effect or the template binding running. The required variants throw when no element matches, also before the first connection: No element matches the required query '…' of <…>, or required content query for content queries.

declaring.title: Declaring queries
declaring.body: The target is a CSS selector or the class of a component (see QueryTarget). A type argument narrows the elements found by a selector; a class gives its instances, with their public members.

whenToRead.title: When to read it
whenToRead.body: A query is empty in onInit and filled before afterRender, then follows the template a microtask behind its changes. Read it in afterRender, in event handlers, or reactively: the computed signals and the effects reading it follow it, and an effect created in onInit runs again when the query is filled. Content queries are still empty in afterRender, since the parent projects the content after the component has rendered.

required.title: Required queries
required.body: The required variants are for an element that is always there: their type has no null, and reading them when nothing matches throws. Reading them in onInit or in the template throws, since the query is filled after the render. Keep the optional variants for an element inside an @if.

EffectOptions.summary: The options of effect() and this.effect(): callbacks around every run of an effect, and at its disposal.
EffectOptions.description: The second argument of effect(), and of this.effect() of components and directives, which pass it on. Every property is optional. Their behavior, with the special cases, is described on the page of effect().

members.onBeforeRun: Called before every run, the first one included.
members.onAfterRun: Called after every run, even when the function of the effect throws.
members.onCleanup: Called when the effect is disposed, not between one run and the next.

InputSignalOptions.summary: The options of an input: the options of a signal, plus transform, converting the values the templates bind.
InputSignalOptions.description:
The options accepted by @Property and @Property.required, together with alias, for the InputSignal they create. ActualValue is the type of the input, IncomingValue the type of the values bound to it: the same, unless transform converts them.

equals, watched and unwatched come from SignalOptions, and work as the options of signal().

members.transform:
Converts every value a template binds, static or computed by an expression, before it is compared with equals and stored. It does not run on the default value, nor when the input goes back to it because a conditional binding stopped holding.

It does not change the type the templates are checked against: that is ActualValue, the type of the InputSignal, not the parameter of transform. A transform from string to number does not allow a static value on an input typed number: prefer transforms keeping the type, which trim or normalize the value, and bind expressions.
members.equals: Compares the value returned by transform with the current one: when it returns true, the input keeps its value and notifies nobody. It also decides whether going back to the default value is a change. The default is Object.is, so a new array with the same content is a change.
members.watched: Called when the input gets its first dependent, with the signals frozen. See signal().
members.unwatched: Called when the input loses its last dependent, with the signals frozen. See signal().

passing.title: Passing the options
passing.body: The options are the second argument of @Property, after the default value, and the only one of @Property.required.

QueryTarget.summary: What a query looks for: a CSS selector, the class of a component, or the class of a custom directive.
QueryTarget.description:
The first argument of every @Query decorator. A view query looks only in the shadow root of its component, a content query only among the elements projected into it, or in its light DOM: neither finds the elements inside the shadow root of a child component.

The target also decides the type of the elements found: see QueryElement.

members.selector: Any CSS selector, as querySelector accepts it: a tag name (input, ex-badge), a class (.row), an attribute ([item]), or a combination of them. The elements found are typed HTMLElement, unless the decorator gets a narrower type as its first type argument, as in @Query<HTMLInputElement>('input').
members.class:
The class of a component decorated with @WebComponent: the query looks for the selector of the component, and the elements found are typed as instances of the class, with its public members.

Any class extending HTMLElement type-checks, but a class without a selector, such as a native class like HTMLInputElement, makes the query throw when the component declaring it is created.
members.directive: The class of a CustomDirective: the query holds the instances of the directive, and of its subclasses, applied to the elements it looks into, rather than the elements. A directive applied with @@selector and a host directive of a component are both found.

kinds.title: A target of each kind
kinds.body: A selector, a selector with the type of the element, the class of a component, and a selector for all the matches.

QueryElement.summary: The type of each element a query finds, worked out from its target.
QueryElement.description:
For a QueryTarget that is a CSS selector, it is ElementType: the decorators pass their first type argument, HTMLElement by default. For the class of a component, it is the instance type of the class, and ElementType is ignored.

The @Query decorators use it to type their signals, such as QuerySignal<QueryElement<Target, ElementType> | null> for @Query: code rarely needs to write it.

resolving.title: How it resolves
resolving.body: Written by hand, it takes both type arguments.

QuerySlotOptions.summary: The options of the content queries: which slots to look into, or the whole light DOM instead.
QuerySlotOptions.description: The second argument of @Query.content, @Query.content.required and @Query.content.all (see @Query). Without options, a content query looks among the elements assigned to any slot of the component, and their descendants. slots restricts it to some slots, lightDom extends it to the whole light DOM of the element: the type does not allow both.

members.slots:
The name of the slot to look into, or a list of names, where the empty string is the default slot. When it is omitted, every slot is.

The results follow the slots in the order of the template, then the elements in the order they were assigned, each followed by its matching descendants. A slot forwarding the content of another slot is flattened, and the fallback content of the slots is never found. An empty list matches no slot.
members.lightDom: When true, the query looks among all the descendants of the element in the light DOM, assigned to a slot or not, in document order, and runs again only when elements are added or removed. Defaults to false.

choosing.title: Choosing the slots
choosing.body: Content queries with each option, and a combination that does not compile.

QueryOptions.summary: The options of the queries holding a single element: what they read from the element they find.
QueryOptions.description: The second argument of @Query, @Query.required, @Query.ref and @Query.ref.required, and, together with QuerySlotOptions, of @Query.content and @Query.content.required (see @Query). The .all variants take no read.

members.read: What the query holds for the element it finds, see QueryRead. By default the element, or the instance of the directive when the target is the class of a directive.

reading.title: Reading a directive or an element
reading.body: A directive read from the element a selector or a ref finds, the element a directive is applied to, the option among the options of the slots, and a variant that does not take it.

QueryRead.summary: What a query reads from the element it finds: the element, or the instance of a directive applied to it.
QueryRead.description: The type of the read option of the queries holding a single element (see QueryOptions). It types what the query holds: 'element' by the type argument of the decorator, a directive as an instance of its class.

members.element: The element itself. It changes the result only when the target is the class of a directive, which otherwise holds the instance of the directive: with 'element' the query holds the element it is applied to.
members.directive: The class of a CustomDirective: the query holds the instance applied to the element, with @@selector or as a host directive, or of a subclass. The elements without it are skipped.
